utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Lausic, again I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you would speak the truth the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Mr. Misetic are you ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I am, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me take you back to where we left off last night to refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit P877 on the screen, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, again, just this is to refresh your recollection, but this is the order that you issued on 18th August following your receipt of the letter from Mr. Moric on the 17th, and you issued it to all of the military police battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if I could now have Exhibit D1071, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the report, the next day, issued to you or sent to you by the commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, Mr. Budimir, directly to you, pursuant to the order you had issued the day before requiring implementation of certain measures and requiring a report back to you about the implementation of the measures in your order. And in the -- it begins, he specifically cites the fact that you had issued the order and that he was acting pursuant to that order and that it was concerning the most efficient possible cooperation with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And he reports on what he had done pursuant to your order. He says meeting were held in point 1 with the head of the police sector in Split of the police administration, joint check-points were agreed, joint patrols in the newly liberated territories. He tells you that in Sinj there was a meeting between a Mr. Mate Bilobrk and Captain Jenic of the 5th Company. Joint action in all segments as in Item 1 of this order was agreed, laying emphasis on control of road traffic. In point 3, again similar meetings in Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn the page please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then he reports in point 4 that a meeting wasn't held in the Zadar-Knin police administration because Mr. Ivica Cetina, the head of the police administration, he had orders to establish contact at the level of command of the 71st and 72nd Battalions and no orders on establishing contact at the lower levels. Now, from Mr. Budimir's report, did you conclude that in fact Mr. Budimir had compiled with your order?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can see, all of the points of my order were implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you note from the report that Mr. Budimir is reporting directly to you and is not copying anyone else on what he was doing to implement your order. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One cannot see that from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar, if we could have Exhibit D1072 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is your order from the 30th of August. The subject again is coordinates meetings with members of the MUP regarding more effective cooperation and joint consideration. And you reference a 1994 order, and then again the 18 August order that we've seen this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You, in the preamble say: "After successfully carrying out Operation Storm, all military police units, expect for the 68th, established full military and police control over their areas of responsibility. "Consequently commanders of these military police units are responsible for maintaining public law and order, crime control, and security of road traffic for members of the Croatian army. They will ensure that these tasks are carried out by executing the authority of the military police and working in close coordination with commanders of police stations and chiefs of police administrations ..." Now, that was an accurate statement of fact that it was the commanders of the military police units that were responsible for maintaining public law and order, crime control, and security of road traffic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In keeping with the tasks and scope of activity of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You then issue an order and you say that: "In their areas of responsibility, commanders of the military police units shall determine the levels of coordination meetings (platoon commanders - to commanders of the police stations, company commanders to the chiefs of the police stations) and ensure that they take place every week. At these meetings, the following issues should be analysed in detail: The security situation in the area of responsibility; work and cooperation between patrol and policing services, check-points, on-site investigations ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we have an accurate translation there, Mr. President, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "Forensic anlayses, control and regulation of military road traffic; joint review of demobilization of HV units," et cetera, et cetera. At point 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Daily exchange of daily reports, an unobstructed system of communications between duty services, and prompt response following a call by a duty service of the police station, police administration, and the other way around." Point 4 you say: "I hereby hold commanders of the VP battalions and VP independent companies responsible for failure to hold cooperation meetings or failing to have effective and practical cooperation." It is then forwarded also to Mr. Moric, Mr. Rebic, and the chiefs of the departments of the military police administration. Again, this was an order, your effort, your attempt, to improve the general level of security in the liberated territories. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That was one of the efforts we put in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you were implementing your efforts through your battalion commanders in the field. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And to do that, there was no need to copy anyone in the military line on this order.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, it was sent to the MOD, which then to my superior, who was assistant commander for security, as well as to the chiefs of sectors in the MP administration. That is to say, the people from the profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, not the MOD, but the Ministry of Interior, in the first line of the -- in the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, let me turn your attention to another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And this, Mr. Registrar, is 65 ter 5803, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: These are the working minutes of a briefing that was held in Split by MP unit commanders on the 7th of September, although the minutes were formally completed on the 22nd of September which is why that date is in the upper left-hand corner. But if you look at the introduction, it says there was a briefing by the MP unit commanders regarding the work of the military police during the months of July and August, which was held on 7 September 1995 in Split. I checked in your notes for that day, Mr. Lausic, and it appears that, in fact, in your notes you also reflect that you were present at this meeting. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. Just a small correction. Mr. Misetic said working minutes, I think he meant minutes from the working meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, a slip of the tongue. I'll try not to pull a Kehoe again, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page, Mr. Lausic, I'll have the Registrar turn the page in both English and Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says as you can see: "The following persons attended," and you are at number one. Do you recall the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I can also find it in my diary. It started at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Also present, and we can scroll through here, is your deputy chief, Mr. Biskic. At number 4, Major Juric. At number 5, Captain Eljuga, acting chief of the criminal military police. If we can turn the page in English, please. At number 15, Colonel Mihael Budimir, commander of the 72nd MP Battalion, is present. And then the minutes reflect that you held the introduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn the page in Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You said on behalf of the military police administration, and then your personal name, congratulate the military police unit commanders on completion of all tasks which were assigned to them as part of the Operation Oluja. And then the minutes reflect at the bottom of the English page that the first thing discussed was the preparations for a sports games. Do you recall the military police in early September was involved in providing security for a sporting event? I'm sorry, I didn't hear your answer. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Starting with 1992, every year, one MP unit organised sport games for the armed forces in the Republic of Croatia. There were sport games for MP units. In 1995, the fourth military police sports games were organised by the 72nd MP Battalion. The games were held in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now after that discussion there is the -- the reports from each battalion commander were provided about what they had done in July and August as well as assessments by the military police administration officers about the work of that particular battalion. And so I'd like to call your attention to the report and assessment of the 72nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if I could turn the page, this is numbered page 15 at the bottom, which should be the same in the e-court. Right? And page 11 in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we scroll to the bottom in English, he started off talking about the participation of the 72nd Battalion in Operation Ljeto 95 or Summer 95. And the work of the anti-terrorist company. And then in the third paragraph -- or second paragraph from the bottom in Croatian and the last paragraph in the English, he reported at this meeting 250 men took part in the combat activities during the Operation Oluja. It is being noted that there were instances of setting fires to houses in the area of" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "... responsibility of the 72nd Military Police Battalion. However, after the initial four to five days, all such occurrences were prevented." And then in the last paragraph of his briefing, he says: "As far as the cooperation with other police administrations is concerned, there were some problems in this area, but these problems should be solved after the meeting with Split-Dalmatia police administration chief."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can scroll down in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now this is where the administration officers assess -- provide their assessment of the work of the 72nd. And Major Juric says: "There are no objections to the report itself, nor are there any objections to the work of the traffic military police. The unit has accepted the new system of reporting, both in terms of monthly and daily reports."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He says, He, himself, was present in the area of responsibility of the 72nd Battalion at the time. It is his opinion that all services OVP, PVP, and criminal military police carried out their taskings successfully and very professionally and that all of them deserved to be commended. Captain Grancaric and Captain Mrkota were commended. The next entry is by Captain Eljuga, the acting chief of the crime police in the administration, with regards to the work of the criminal military police: "There are no objections. All tasks were completed on time and with high degree of quality. The monthly report is good and encompasses all the areas. There is, however, a single observation; namely, in one of the tables, the number of criminal charges is 29, while in another, the number is 22, which creates some confusion. However, this can be easily resolved by a phone call." Now, if we can go to page 18 in the English for the assessment provided by your deputy, Deputy Chief Mr. Biskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which I think is the next page in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "In relation to the overview of the public law and order violations, security, military traffic, and crime, every unit in its zone of responsibility must precisely state from which HV unit comes a person involved in a traffic accident, JRM violation or a criminal act. This is because of the fact that, so far, certain mistakes have been occurring. Namely, an overview of a situation in a zone of responsibility would be presented and attributed accordingly to a Military District, whereas a large number of HV members who reported themselves" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I think that is probably not the best translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But: "... who reported themselves as perpetrators of certain actions do's not belong to the said Military District." Now, Mr. Lausic, you're present at the meeting based on the reports of Mr. Budimir as well as the assessments provided by the various department chiefs of the military police administration. Did you agree with the assessments of the status and state of events in the zone of responsibility of the 72nd Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As any other minutes, these minutes merely note the words spoken by the rapporteur. I wouldn't be able to tell you if I agree or disagree on the basis of the text here. I can't merely reduce it down to a discussion noted down by the note keeper 14 years later. This isn't a round table. It is after all a hearing of a witness before the ICTY. I can't only comment on the minutes. Whoever had something to say, put forth their opinion. It was taken down in the minutes, and the minutes were delivered to all participants in the meeting. You have my view expressed as contained in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to assume that the minute taker, if the chief of the military police administration criticised the persons and their reports as being inaccurate, would have recorded that in the minutes of the meeting. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, the various interventions were noted down but not in the form of a stenogram or a transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, let me ask one final question on this point. You attended enough meetings; you have seen enough minutes of meetings; you have a general understanding of what would or wouldn't be in the minutes of a meeting. If you criticised the assessments of Mr. Budimir, Mr. Eljuga, Mr. Juric, Mr. Biskic, those criticisms would certainly have been in the minutes that were put together. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, two days ago I said that I am hesitant to answer hypothetical questions: What would happen if this and that were happening? We have the minutes. The minutes contain the words spoken by the participants. You have my introductory word there. There are no comments or opinions expressed -- or, rather, formulated in the minutes. Fourteen years later it is very difficult for me to make any sort of comments in relation to the minutes. At some -- at times the minutes would have the form that they have now. At other times they would be in the form of a transcript where you would be able to get an idea of what the comments were like. The minute-taker, the note-taker taking these particular minutes was not a professional. It was a secretary, an administrative secretary, who did the best she could under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender 65 ter 5803 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1286.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could please have Exhibit P2166.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, I'd like to take you to your diary of the 13th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, this is at page 65 in the English and page 59 in the B/C/S. If we can go down to Mr. Moric's section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, you'll recall that you were asked questions by Mr. Tieger about this and then extensively by the Presiding Judge about this entry, and I'd now like to take you back. And while you can't remember what was said at the 7th of September meeting in Split, you did provide some interpretations of Mr. Moric's thoughts on the 13th of September. And now let's take a look at -- again, what Mr. Moric said. If we go to the fourth point he says: "The line of command is not operational. Since on the level of the Military Districts, they believe that they are either misinformed or that things are misrepresented or misinterpreted. We must make sure military commanders know the truth." Now, I'd like to take you to the transcript of your questions and answers by Judge Orie. That question and answer session begins at page 15324, beginning at line 17. I'd like to take you a question by Judge Orie that begins at 15325 at line 18. Judge Orie asked you: "Now Mr. Moric said that the Military District level believed that they were misinformed or that things were misinterpreted. Did you form an opinion about that as well, whether it was misinformation or -- so not knowing what was actually happening, or was it not wanting to know what was actually happening? Or did you form an opinion about an explanation as to the attitude of the Military District level?" Your answer was: "I personally believe then, as I do now, that commanders at all levels, via the daily and interim reports they received from the military police as well as from their subordinate commanders, did have an opportunity to acquaint themselves with the situation in their respective areas." Then later, at page 15327, beginning at line 16, Judge Orie asks: "And where Moric said that military commanders must know the truth, did you form any opinion as to whether they knew the truth but didn't want to know it? Or that they really did not know the truth and should be informed about what happened?" Your answer: "The same comment would apply to this situation as I said a moment ago. The commanders received reports from MP units from their subordinate officers as well as their assistant commanders in charge of security. And by virtue of those, they had insight into the situation of their respective areas." Mr. Moric -- Mr. Lausic, you have seen from the minutes on the 7th of September that what the military police was reporting, in fact, was that there was some burning in the first four to five days in the area of responsibility of the 72nd, but that now everything was under control. Right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's what Commander Budimir said in his contribution to the discussion, and I can only confirm that these words can be found in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So, therefore, if your answer, at least in part was based on what the military police was reporting to commanders, the military commanders could have concluded that, in fact, if the military police was saying that things were under control, that meant that things were under control. Right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be -- I would be hard-pressed to be expected to know what the assistant commander thought and what sort of opinions he formulated on the basis of the reports he received from the commanders in the field. I did not receive any sort of queries or requests for any answers or for clarification of certain issues from any Military District Commanders throughout the country. That's why it is very difficult for me to tell you what sort of a conclusion a Military District Commander could have arrived at based on the reports he received from a battalion commander of a battalion that was subordinate to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, you were receiving reports obviously. We've seen the reporting you were receiving personally on the 7th. Your conclusion was that things were under control in the 72nd Military Police Battalion on the 7th of September. Correct? Otherwise you would have issued some order on the 7th or taken some measure.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you've put a hypothetical question to me. We've got facts in front of us. The fact is that the meeting was held. The fact is that minutes were made of the commanders' interventions made at the meetings. So what sort of a question am I supposed to answer now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me give you another question, and you said you don't know how you can answer what the Military District Commander may have been thinking. But in your answers to the Presiding Judge about what Mr. Moric may have been thinking, you did provide some answers. And I'm asking you now to look again at Mr. Moric's words, in light of the reporting that the military police was doing, in light of the assessments of the military police on the 7th of September, I'm putting it to you that Mr. Moric was telling you that you were -- and in the military police were misreporting the situation, and that's why he says, We must make sure military commanders must know the truth. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In my diary, there is only one indication of this, a very brief one, concerning what minister Moric had to say. The chain of command is not operational because at the level of the Military District, they believe that they are being misinformed or that something is being misrepresented or misinterpreted. We have to make sure that the commanders know the truth. Now, what was the opinion on the part of Minister Moric that is expressed here? Who is it that is misinforming, misrepresenting, or misinterpreting something? I don't have a note to that effect in my diary, and I can't tell what you it was. Ministry Moric who was also witness who was heard, and perhaps is the one who can answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to, Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 2451, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is from the 12th of September, Mr. Lausic. It is an order again. It's issued to all the military police battalions. And when we get to the back, you'll see that it's issued -- there we go. It's copied to the chiefs of the sections of the military police administration. Now -- actually, I apologise. This is not an order. First you're forwarding something to them, and then there's an order, and we'll get to that order next. But you are forwarding to the MP battalions the analysis of state security -- of the state of security and cooperations between the police and the military police between 22 August and 31 August. And you say: "Please find attached the analysis of the reports submitted by the police administrations referring to setting houses on fire, removal of other people's items, cooperation with the military police, and measures taken in that respect. "The above mentioned analysis is to be closely studied and joint actions should be discussed and measures set out at coordination meetings, in order to make the cooperation more effective and raise the security in general on a higher level." And then the analysis from each of the police administrations is attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we go to the last page or second to last page, which is page eight in the English. Page 7 in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You have some statistics. A survey of criminal acts per police administration. For that week, for example, in Knin you have 24 arsons, no explosions, no removal of movables. The police administration Zadar-Knin, 47 arsons, 8 removal of movables. And then a survey of on-site investigation and structure of perpetrators. For Zadar-Knin, 55 on-site investigations, 9 HV members identified as the perpetrates. Sibenik, 48 investigations, 8 HV members. Split-Dalmatia, 1 investigation, 5 HV members. And I'll ask you a question after I show you the nest document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. President, if I could tender 65 ter 2451, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's an item on the bar table, Your Honours, so I presume there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is document shall be given Exhibit D1287.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. It's on the bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on the bar table, then I misunderstood you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Correction for the transcript. This document shall not be given Exhibit D1287. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The number is vacated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could, Mr. Registrar, have 65 ter 2482, please. That's 65 ter 2482. I'm sorry, Mr. Registrar, it's 65 ter 2842.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is your order of the 12th of September, following that correspondence from the MUP. And in the preamble you begin write: "Having analysed the work of the MP units mostly in the newly liberated areas ... we came to the conclusion that the check-points on the entrances to the newly liberated areas are not efficient, that the military police motorised units were not assigned to the specific tasks or patrol areas," and then you issue an order. In point 1 you revoke the order of the 14th of August, which establishes check-points at the entrance and exit from the newly liberated areas. And you instruct the military police to advise or inform the heads of the police administrations and the police units about removing the check-points. You institute a new system of patrolling in point 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The report in point 3 is: "The report" -- I'm sorry. Finishing in point 2: "The entire area of responsibility should be covered by patrolling areas. Timely interventions as requested by MUP check-points shall be secured through uninterrupted radio contact with the MUP patrols and through visits to the MUP check-points." And then ask you for a report to be submitted to you about patrol strength and structure, equipment, code-names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The working radio channel of the patrols, and that the report should be submitted by 1200 hours on the 16th of September. And if you see who you copied on this, it's the military police administration departments, the military police administration sections, and Mr. Moric. Now, again, this is at a time after your discussions with Mr. Moric as reflected in your diary. You used your authority under Article 8 of the rules to take measures and give instructions to the military police for more effective use of the military police on the ground. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. A new method of proceeding, in order to be more efficient in our cooperation with the colleagues from the Ministry of Interior because as we were able to see from this analysis that was received from the -- for the period between the period between the 22nd and 31st August, the situation was not good and, we, together with our colleagues from the MUP, tried to find out the ways that would be best to counter these incidents. Item 4 of this order, which you didn't read, stated that the regular and traffic military police department officers and department chiefs would be in charge of controlling and implementing the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, unless it's on the bar table, I tender 65 ter 2842.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not on the bar table. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, this document would receive ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall receive Exhibit D1287. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1287 is admitted into evidence. Perhaps, Mr. Lausic, could you tells what NUVP means. In the translation that isn't -- the interpreters did not know what it stands for.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Chief of the administration of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lausic, I'd like to take you back to Exhibit D567, which is your 16 September report to General Cervenko. And this is your analysis of the use of the military police of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia in Operation Storm on the 16th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 8 in the English, which is numbered paragraph 6.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And again you write: "In larger villages and towns, and along major roads, constant beat patrols ensured law and order, prevented torching and the uncontrolled removal of war booty, and controlled the safety of military road traffic." Would you agree that that assessment was consistent with the assessments that were provided in the meeting in Split on the 7th of September about the situation in the zone of the 72nd Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the one that the commander of the 72nd Battalion referred to when he was speaking or ... or are you referring to what I referred to in the introduction to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the assessment by the commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion as well as the administration officers who provided their own assessments of the situation in the 72nd Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know who or what is producing some additional --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour, I'm sorry. I just accidentally pushed the wrong button.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Never do that, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must confess, not fully. This is my report, and you want me to put that in relation with -- or to somebody's briefing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me say that your report is based on the reports of and the assessments provided to you by all of your subordinates. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report was drafted pursuant to the reports received from the specialties departments of the MP administration. And this is my summary reports that I submitted to the addressees that can you see. The way in which the chiefs of specialised departments of the MP administration received information is, I suppose, through the professional services, along the chain of reporting. Therefore, I can only comment the part that I signed and which is basically my report, and I can verify it as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you, then, the more general question. You reported this to General Cervenko, and I assume that you still believe that the military police beat patrols ensured law and order, prevented torching and the uncontrolled removal of war booty, and controlled the safety of military road traffic. Was that an accurate assessment at that time you wrote this in September 1995?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In item 6.3, the task is not referred to as completed but something that is ongoing. This is not in past tense. It is in the present tense, and the exact wording is that in larger settlements and cities and along the roads, beat and patrol service is ensured on a constant basis to establish law and order. And this is referred to a process -- this refers to a process which had not been completed by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, but, Mr. Lausic, the point of the report is, in fact, to provide an assessment looking back from the beginning of Operation Storm and how Operation Storm and afterwards were conducted, right, that's the point of why you're preparing a report titled "analysis of the use of the military police in Operation Storm"?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. On page 1, just below where it says "Minister of Defence and chief of the Main Staff," as well as the subject which is "analysis of work of the military police," a reference is made. I stated what the analysis of mine was based on. That was based on the order of the chief of the Main Staff of the 8th of September, 1995, ordering that such anlayses be provided, in order for a final analysis to be conducted at the level of the Main Staff. I believe it was subsequently done. This was supposed to be material for that analysis that was to be conducted at the level of the ministry and the staff on Operation Storm. I believe it was done towards the end of September. I probably have that in my notes, and I was probably present at such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, just generally speaking then. Let me put it a different way. If there was a problem and the military police had been unable to ensure law and order in the liberated territories from the 4th of August to the 16th of September, you would have put that in this report somewhere. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, again you are putting questions which -- well, I won't call them hypothetical. But we are -- we should stick to the facts. We have this report. I signed it and sent it on. There are stipulations contained therein which I can confirm as mine, and I had verified them. Had some other circumstances prevailed, other things would have been mentioned, but we have what we have. I confirm that this is my report sent to the addressees mentioned in the course of preparation for an analysis to be conducted at the level of the ministry and the Main Staff. Fourteen years down the road, I no longer remember whether I wanted to add something but did not, or whether I skipped something. This is the only copy we have. I no longer have my working copies, and this report stands as a fact, full stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I understand. What I'm basically interested in knowing is your position on the following question: In this document, your conclusion was that the military police was able to maintain law and order.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing we can find in the document is that the military police was performing those tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Lausic, let me turn your attention then to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask a few clarifying questions here, Mr. Lausic. We've seen this meeting where Mr. Budimir reports that, apart from the first four or five days, that incidents of -- of torching did not occur after that. That would bring us somewhere to 10th of August, approximately. Of course, this Chamber has received quite a bit of evidence, and to say that no arson or torching was ever in this evidence after the 10th of August would, I think would not be correct. Now, Mr. Budimir says everything under control in the area of responsibility of the 72nd Military Police Battalion. In your report here, you use different language. You say: "In larger villages and towns and along major roads, constant beat patrols ensured law and order." Now you can look at it in two different ways. Fine, everything is under control, more or less in line with what Mr. Budimir said. You also could read it that, although matters may be under control in larger villages and towns and along major roads, that the same might not be true in smaller villages and on the minor roads. I'm trying to interpret your words here. Do I have to read in 6.3 everything is fine; or should I also read in 6.3, Well, we exercise control in major villages and towns, but we have to limit it to that because the same is not true for smaller villages and for roads not mentioned here. Could you clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The term used, "in larger settlements and cities and along roads," should include the areas of our activity. As to whether the beat patrol services went to remote villages or hamlets is something I cannot tell you. I have to remind you, though, that the area was extensively mined and our movements had to be limited to the areas which were safe for traffic. That is probably why I used the terminology "in larger settlements along roads," et cetera, et cetera. This was a newly liberated area contaminated with mines and explosives, unsafe for movement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you there. I do understand that due to the situation with mines that you might not have been able to go everywhere. Nevertheless, one of the by-products of arson and torching is smoke. So even if you don't come that close, you can observe sometimes that you see smoke at a distance and, of course, could be a haystack that went on fire. But sometimes you have indications. Now what I would like it know: Did you have any indications at that time as whether or not the areas you didn't come closer that torching and arson may well have occurred, or at least that fires occurred where you couldn't come close enough to establish whether it was arson or whether it was fire by other causes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the reports I received daily from the duty service, such events were recorded, to the effect that patrols noticed smoke drills but that they were unable to access the area in order to establish what the situation was. One of the most common reasons was that patrols stipulated that the areas were dangerous because of the mines and minefields present there. Sometimes in the reports one would find sentences to the effect that patrols, in the course of the night, noticed fires. But given the fact that they did not have vehicles, they could not go to investigate. Frequently they also lacked means of communication to be able to report that to a superior level. In a number of circumstances, also the human factor, that is fear, caused the lack of activity, in order to go and try to establish what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because in this report and, for example, in paragraph 6.3, it's very positively phrased, Look at what we do. Or, Look at what we've done. Whereas now you say, Well, the job hadn't finished yet; the report is not only looking back. And also, from what you tell us now, the situation was not to be interpreted as positively as perhaps the language here suggests. Is that a fair interpretation of this type of reporting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the events that were recorded in the course of the first few days, by the point when this draft -- report was drafted, things were being brought under control and improving. The security situation was being improved from one day to the next. This report also has that overtone, in the sense that we were doing our best to improve the situation, which has been -- had been improved by that point already. However, one cannot be completely satisfied as a policeman, ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if Mr. Budimir reports that after the first four, five days, similar occurrences could be prevented, I do understand that you would not share that optimistic view that such things didn't occur anymore after the first four or five days, although you said the situation improved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this report covers the entire 8.000 square kilometres of the newly liberated area, with all of the characteristics which prevailed and which can be seen from the analysis we received from our colleagues from the Ministry of the Interior. The report mentions the various police administrations in which the situation differed. If we look at the statistics on arson, explosions, scene of crime investigations, and the structure of perpetrators, we have all that data there. By virtue of my analysis, I tried to unify all of the information to cover the entire newly liberated area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... a rather long question, and even if Mr. Budimir may have limited him to the area of responsibility for the 72nd Military Police Battalion, I do understand from your answers that you certainly, for the whole of the activities of the military police covered by this report, that you wouldn't confirm then nothing happened anymore after the first four or five days. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually, I think -- concerning this document, let me just take you to the proposals which are on page 10. Although you have now stated that by this time the situation was in fact improving and had improved by that point already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Page 9 in the original, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your first recommendation is about having meetings with commanders with the Ministry of Interior, et cetera. And you have testified that -- actually it says, "which would be held in the coming period," but there was a proposal that you made for purposes of coordination. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And is this proposal similar to the proposal that you made -- or, I'm sorry, order that you made on the 18th of August where you wanted your military policemen to get the telephone numbers of commanders. You said it was for the purpose of knowing where units might be and having better information about movements. Was that the purpose of having commanders attend these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Misetic. In this proposal, it is proposed that the most senior commander; that is to say, the Military District Commander, as well as an officer of the SIS and an officer from political affairs, at the highest level, should meet with the assistant ministers; that is to say, Mr. Moric, and Mr. Benko, in all districts of the -- of the Croatian army covering the area -- newly liberated area in its entirety in order to take on responsibility for the behaviour of HV members as well as to use the chain of command to supervise the movement of those members. I believe two days ago that I told you that, as far as I know, such meetings were not held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your witness statement at paragraph 251, which is at page 52 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And that is Exhibit P2159.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You -- in the -- in the middle of that paragraph you say: "During the course of Operation Storm and its aftermath, I had no contact with General Gotovina about any crimes or problems with the military. I have never had any conversation with General Gotovina about problems that occurred after the operation."

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please tell me again what the number of the paragraph in the statement is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 251. And, again, it's in the -- beginning around the middle of the paragraph. Can you find it, Mr. Lausic?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's also on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's easier for me to read it in my copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was that statement true?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to refer to the stenogram, the transcript of my suspect interview. Perhaps this is just a brief form of the same, but I see nothing that would be in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, the investigator's question was whether I visited the area of the Split Military District and Knin specifically, and I think this was my answer, that I did not go to that area but to some other area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now we've seen many documents that you are, for example, issuing orders and sending directly copies to the Split Military District command. If necessary, I can show you other documents -- and I'm sure you probably have recollection that there would, on occasion, be direct communication between you and General Gotovina about, for example, the use of the anti-terrorist platoon. Do you recall that General Gotovina would approach you about being able to use the anti-terrorist platoon and asking that it be subordinated to him? For example, in your diary, I believe in April 29, you can see an entry where General Gotovina's request was approved?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 29th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was before Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me not confuse you. In the course of your career and General Gotovina's career, you had direct communications with each other when necessary. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we came across each other, be it officially or unofficially or by chance or as agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But you could also have direct correspondence with each other if it was necessary?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, my question to you is: If you felt there was a problem in the line of command of General Gotovina concerning criminality, and you felt that he could do something about it -- let me ask the preliminary question. Did you feel that there was a problem in the line of command of General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No more or less compared to all other Military District Commanders. In other areas, we had identical situations basically, judging by the daily reports as we did in his area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If there was something specific that needed to be addressed by General Gotovina that was urgent, you would have and could have written to him directly and proposed some specific measure. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had received a notification from my battalion commander and when the forward command post of the MP administration headed by Major Juric was still in existence, pointing to the fact that there were problems in the area of responsibility of a given Military District Commander, for example, that he rejected our proposals or behaved of his own free accord, then I would have done something but through the Main Staff, or at least with them being informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive a note official from the battalion commander or Major Juric about General Gotovina rejecting your proposals or behaving of his own free accord?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this might be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could I ask one clarifying question before we go to the break. We have dealt with -- Mr. Misetic has dealt with your notes about this meeting where Mr. Moric and -- where you write down that Mr. Moric said that they should know the truth, and you said, Well, I formed an opinion about it as well. So apparently whether misreporting or for whatever other reason, you were both were concerned about the military command structure not knowing the truth. Did you ever consider to communicate with Mr. Gotovina or anyone in his line of command to say, Whether you misunderstand our reports or whatever it may be, but please be aware this and this is the case. I think that Mr. Misetic is asking whether such direct communications whether they ever were there and whether you have ever considered. Because apparently from what I read, that was of great concern to you, to you both.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my point of contact was the chief of the Main Staff of the armed forces, assistant minister for security, and the minister of defence. Had it been mentioned in the report of Major Juric or from the commander of the 72nd Battalion that the Military District Commander had from his level resisted such proposals and everything else that would call for the higher level to intervene, of course, I would have, through the chief of the Main Staff, made that contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would not have directly contacted, if there were any concern in this respect, with Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I always tried to honour the chain of command, i.e., to make sure that the higher level was always aware of the problem before the problem itself reached the level which would have been duty-bound to report on that problem. That was what I always tried to observe in the reporting system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. We'll have a break and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, and perhaps totally superfluous. Mr. Tieger, the deadline for applications for protective measures, if needed at all, under in -- in relation to the decision on 92 quater witnesses, the deadline, today's the last day. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could go back to D567, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: While we're getting that up on the screen, Mr. Lausic, I want to give you an opportunity. The Presiding Judge asked you a question about if -- if there was fire after Operation Storm spotted, for example, in an outlying village and how the military police might react. Could you give us a brief explanation as to the relationship and authorities of the civilian police after Operation Storm, and the military police, as you understood it, after Operation Storm. What was the job of the civilian police on the liberated territory; and what was the job of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely on the day that Minister Jarnjak publically stated in Knin at a press conference, or at any rate, over the media, that the civilian authority has become operational in the newly liberated area and that all the various civilian structures are functional in the liberated area. It is also stated that the ministry of the interior was the one that had the competence to maintain public law and order and to prevent all sorts of crime. It was primarily charged with maintaining a state of security in the newly liberated area. However, in view of the fact that there was a large presence of the HV units in the area at that time, it was only natural that the military police force would have and maintain a larger presence in the area. As one could see in all the documents presented, in all our contacts, we, as services in charge of the security of the Republic of Croatia and as part of the security system of the Republic of Croatia, tried to do the maximum given our human and materiel resources to bring the security level in Croatia as high up as possible. In answer to your question, or, rather, the question of the Presiding Judge, that a military police patrol may have spotted a fire, well, in that case, had that been the case, they would have and, of course, we have to keep in mind that the area was mined, made sure to check up on what had had happened. If the patrol in that case caught red-handed either a member -- members of the military police or civilians, it would have been duty-bound to act. If the police came across civilians committing that crime, they would keep them in custody and notify the civilian police which would have taken over the criminal investigation. If it caught red-handed the HV members, then the military police would carry out its own investigations, notify all the necessary levels and process the case. The same would apply if a civilian police patrol caught either HV members or civilians perpetrating an offence. They would be duty-bound to take the same steps. If the perpetrators are soldiers, then they would notify the military police which would then take its further steps; and if the perpetrators were civilians, then the civilian police itself would do its job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could go to paragraph 6.3 again. Page 8 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, above paragraph 6.3, in your report you note that: "The anti-terrorist platoon of the 72nd VP Battalion continued its engagement in combat operations under the direct command of the Split Military District commander and participated in Operation Maestral." This report -- first, you were aware that obviously that the HV was conducting military operations in Bosnia at the time of the writing of this report?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you were aware at the time of the writing of this report that it was General Gotovina who was commanding those operations in Bosnia at the time of this report. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if I could take you to your diary, which is P2166, B/C/S page 35, English page 39. Which is your entry for August 10th. I want to, again, make sure that I understood your testimony before the break correctly. You never received any information that there was a problem with General Gotovina in the Split Military District. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean personally from General Gotovina, that I should have received reports about problems from him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying is, I think you testified before that neither from Mr. Budimir or Mr. Juric did you receive any indication that there was a problem with General Gotovina's command in the Split Military District. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, just to clarify a matter - and if we can scroll down - and you were asked about there by Mr. Tieger on direct. This is on the 10th at 2100, and it was in relation to this incident in Gospic but your -- it says: "Informed the commander of the Gospic Military District Staff Brigadier Mirko Norac ordered the arrest of a larger group of members of one battalion of the 118th Brigade." And if we could turn the page, please. "Home Guard Regiment who refused to follow orders." And then it says: "Following consultations with the Main Staff of the HV staff Brigadier Mato Obradovic and personally with staff Brigadier Mirko Norac, it was decided not to carry out the arrests, but instead to let the tension die down." Now that's one example of you having a direct communication with a Military District Commander where there was a problem. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But previously, with the person number one of the Main Staff. The way the Main Staff worked was that the operation centre and the duty officer of the operation centre of the Main Staff would be replacing the chief of the Main Staff during his shift, and he would be officer number one of the Main Staff at the time. I may have talked to the duty officer of the operation centre with the duty officer Staff Brigadier Obradovic and conveyed to him the information I received from the commander of the 71st Battalion. And upon consultations with him, it was decided that the most appropriate course of action, in view of the problem that had arisen, that I should make contact with the commander of the Gospic Military District Brigadier Mirko Norac, and try and resolve the problem to make sure that the tensions eased and to avoid the use of measures that might have far-reaching consequences. But let me state again that before talking to the Gospic Military District Commander, I talked to the Main Staff. And that's what I said earlier on, that the first contact and the main level was that of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, first, are you aware that in that period when in your diary you're talking with Mr. Moric, being, let's say, around the 10th of September to the 16th of September, that General Gotovina, at that time, was in Bosnia conducting Operation Maestral?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't state with any precision if I was aware of the dynamics of the various operations in Bosnia, which were led by General Gotovina and with his participation. But, of course, I knew that operations were under way, and that the commander of these operations was General Gotovina. However, I can't pinpoint the exact periods or dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if there was a problem that required General Gotovina's attention at that time or that he returned from Bosnia, you would have similarly gone to the Main Staff, whether in writing or orally, and potentially then also tried to talk to General Gotovina personally if, in fact, you had any information that there was a problem. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not necessary for the Military District Commander to be made contact with. The Military District Commander has his own command and deputy. The Deputy Commander of any level and precisely thus, that a deputy is supposed to stand in for all the functions that the commander has, unlike the assistant commander, who is in charge of only one segment of the areas covered by the commander himself. Therefore, had there been any need for that, which would have been expressed in a report either of the commander of the 72nd Battalion or that of Commander Juric, I would have first contacted the Main Staff and then the command of the Military District. Whether that would be the commander of the district himself or his deputy or a member of the command, that would depend on the requirements of the particular situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, do you ever recall there having been that need and you making such a contact with anyone in the Split Military District command?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could have, please, have Exhibit D595.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, these are the notes of meeting in Plitvice that was held on the 15th of September, between the representatives of the MUP and the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 4 to the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is -- Mr. Budimir was present at this meeting in Plitvice. And in this meeting with Mr. Moric and the members of the MUP and the military police here's what, on the 15th of September, Colonel Budimir said -- is reported to have said that, He called attention to the spatially large area of responsibility covered by the 72nd -- Mr. Lausic, are you looking for your -- are you looking for your copy?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm looking for the notes from my diary because I will be referring to what the minutes have to say on the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what Mr. Budimir said was, He called attention to the spatially large area of responsibility covered by the 72nd Military Police Battalion and did not agree with opinions that there was not enough manpower. The cooperation with the MUP was disturbed but only in some individual cases. The state of security, public order, and road traffic safety reached the satisfying level. And with the return of the civilian population in Knin, a problem with disposal of rubbish occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn the page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First let me ask you this: Do you recall that that's what Mr. Budimir said at that meeting on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The entry for the 15th of September, in my diary, beneath the headline "Colonel Budimir's intervention, the 72nd Battalion," I have only three entries. First one, the number of military policemen is sufficient. So the minutes actually have an inaccurate recording. For the area of Knin, 12 criminal reports were filed. And thirdly, public law and order and the safety of road traffic are currently satisfactory, in contrast to the early days in the wake of the liberation. This is what my diary says, and some of it is contrary to what the minutes have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in the English where it's reported what you said at the meeting. It says: "General Lausic concluded the reports of the Military Police Units' commanders. Members of the MUP and the military police are the promotors of the state policy, and the only people responsible for its implement indication are present at this meeting." Now my first question is: What was the state policy as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, the state policy was reflected in the order which I received as early as -- at first meeting on the 2nd of August in the war conference room. This was a meeting with Minister Susak in preparation of Operation Storm which said that the military police must be more energetic in their activity and prevention. The state policy was also mirrored in all the efforts made by us, the military police, and by the Ministry of Interior, which can be seen from all the various documents with a view to preventing and hindering the commission of criminal offences and to process all the perpetrators, regardless of their provenance. The state policy was also reflected in my proposals which were contained in my reporting to the higher levels of the Ministry of Defence and the armed forces, which had to do with the orders issued down the chain of command, the implementation of which would have -- or would prevent the commission of criminal offences which were not recorded on the ground. And that's what I mean by the state policy. I also refer to that same state policy in my final report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, may I seek one point of clarification. You said, Mr. Lausic, that - let me find it - that you had only three entries in your notebook. And you said, "first one, the number of military policemen is sufficient." And you said: "So the minutes actually have an inaccurate recording." Now, what I see in the minutes is that Mr. Budimir says that he did he not agree with opinions that there was not enough manpower, which suggests that he said, We have sufficient have men. Now, I have difficulties in understanding that you say this is inaccurate apart from the negative formulation. But, for me, it comes down to approximately the same, that, well, whoever says that we haven't got enough men, we have. So I do not see the inaccuracy there, apart from the exact formulation. But could you explain to me what you meant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please scroll down the part that Mr. Budimir was talking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on the top of the page in your language. And in English it's also the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Scroll down, the interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr President, in my diary, the first comment I have next to what Mr. Budimir had to said was, "the number of military policemen was sufficient." That is consistent with what the commander of the 72nd said and which was noted down by the note-taker. That regardless of the fact that the area of responsibility covered by the 72nd Battalion was extensive and large, he did not agree with what was being said, that the manpower levels were insufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, I do not see the inaccuracy in the reporting here because your notes state, although not in exactly the same wording, approximately the same as we find in the notes. This being clarified, please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, I also wanted to ask you about the second portion of that sentence that's ascribed to you, where you said in reference to the state policy: "The only people responsible for its implementation are present at this meeting." You were referring there to the representatives and officials of the MUP and the officials of the military police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if I could have Exhibit P895, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, we've seen Mr. Budimir's assessments from the 7th of September, going into the 15th of September. I'd like to show now an ECMM report of a meeting that was held between General Gotovina and representatives of the ECMM on the 20th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could -- there we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And here's what it is reported General Gotovina to have said at this meeting. "Asked about the ongoing looting arson and harassment, the General's opinion is that the police has to control the situation, and Croatia is still a nation with constitution law and order. Any person committing crimes will be charged. However, a war is always followed by disasters, and now things are under control." Now, you've already talked about this this morning, and you, yourself, said that by the time of your report on the 16th, you felt the situation had improved. But at the time General Gotovina is said to have made this statement, the assessment from the military police, in fact, was that the situation was now under control. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the situation was improving. I think that that was the answer I gave to Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to Exhibit D978, please. It's page 9 in the English version, please. This is not the version I wanted. There it is. If we can go to the paragraph above the section numbered 1.1.4, which I believe is the next page in B/C/S. There.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now this is your annual report for 1995 that was issued in January of 1996. And I'm just going to ask you if you still believe this to be an accurate description. It says: "The control and command system at the level of the military police administration and the daily operations command at the level of the commanders of the Military Districts, the Croatian navy, Croatian air force, and anti-aircraft defence functioned perfectly and received the highest assessment mark in the Flash, Summer 1995, Storm, Maestral, and Southern Stretch offensive operations ..."

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that an accurate description of command and control and the daily operational command functioning perfectly?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That assessment mark was assigned during the analysis of Operations Flash and Storm by the commanders reporting on the execution of their respective tasks in the course of the operations. Also, that was the assessment mark of the MP administration from our level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you go to the next paragraph, it says "coordination." And: "In 1995, commands of military police units compiled work plans in close coordination with commands of the Military Districts, the navy, the air force, and the anti-aircraft defence, garrisons, and other factors influencing the implementation of military police tasks, which enabled effective cooperation in the implementation of tasks, especially during offensive operations of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia." Can you explain what type of coordination is referred to there.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we can see from the report, in item 1.1.4, "coordination," it is stressed that the commanders -- the commands of MP units drafted their work plans in close cooperation with the commands of the Croatian army Military Districts, Croatian navy, Croatian air force, garrisons, et cetera, as well as with other factors influencing the implementation of military police tasks which enabled effective cooperation in the implementation of tasks, especially during offensive operations. In the second paragraph of item 1.1.4, I make note of certain problems, as regards the coordination of tasks at the level of MP units, as well as certain sections and departments of Military Districts, the navy, the air force, and certain administrations of the Main Staff, as well as certain administrations of the Ministry of Defence, logistics bases, et cetera. It was happening because of certain individuals which, by that time, had not grasped the structure of the military police, as well as the prescribed chain of reporting and their obligations towards MP units. I also mentioned that MP units are not part of the Military Districts, navy, the air force. However, it was still the mobilisation development stage of those factors. In the bolded third passage, we express our desire that in 1996, by way of coordination, it should be ensured that the administrations of the Ministry of Defence, of the Main Staff, as well as chiefs of branches and services in the units of Military Districts, the navy, and the air force, it should be ensured that they implement their supervisory role and provide professional help and expertise in order to contribute to the development and work of certain branches and professions within the units of the military police, rather than to merely ask for the implementation of tasks from the scope of work of the military police. In my discussions with the investigators, I used a figure of speech, whereas I said that there was such situations at all levels in which commanders of the HV in their relation to MP units within their area of responsibility, sometimes they behaved as mothers, sometimes as step-mothers. We mentioned something three days ago. It had to do with the case involving the commander of the southern theatre, who used -- or, rather, tried to demobilize a -- a MP unit, which refused his order. In order to further corroborate what I'm talking about in item 1.1.5, which has to do with the supervision of work, in the third bolded passage, I stress that there was no supervision of the work of MP units from the level of district -- Military District commands, the command of the navy, and the command of the air force, as well as the professional administrations of the Main Staff, and there was no -- there were no inspections carried out by the main inspectorate of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, the witness now referred to the third bold paragraph of 1.1.4, which does not appear on our screen and is not uploaded in e-court. We now move to 1.1.5 which is also not uploaded, at least not in translation into e-court. So I have great difficulties in following the explanation of paragraphs which I can't read in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. President, I was asking him about one portion, and it was a 65 ter exhibit that this translation included, so I guess we will have to ask for the entire translation of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's' a very lengthy document from what I'm aware of, so I'm not insisting on having the whole of the document translated, but at least the paragraphs in relation to which the witness gives evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I'm a bit puzzled anyhow, because this piece of translation is -- as it is uploaded in e-court at this moment, which is a -- I have one -- there's a full translation uploaded of the -- of the table of contents which follows a three pages of kind of cover pages, so it's a six-page document. And I'm just trying to find ... the original uploaded is in e-court, 54 pages. And then we have another -- oh, no, suddenly the ... yes, and then we have the three pages translation which I can now access in e-court going up to and including 114 which was previously not accessible to me. So it is an incomplete record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. We will get a translation of those sections as well uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, let me turn your attention again to Exhibit P2189, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President. Could I be permitted to complete the sentence I began while quoting paragraph 1.1.5 of this annual report? I believe it to be important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Our problem is that we have no paragraph 1.1.5 available.
