If you think that paragraph 1.1.5 is of great importance, then Mr. Misetic is invited to at least take care that 1.1.5 is translated as quickly as possible so that can you revisit it. But the Chamber has difficulties in receiving evidence and comment on a document which is -- which the Chamber can't read. But Mr. Misetic has an opportunity to -- before you leave, to address the matter. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This, again, is the Operative Action Varivode. We saw that on Wednesday together. Let me -- you -- as we recall, you put together a team of people to begin conducting investigations about allegations of murder. First, I note that in Operative Action Varivode, this was a coordinated action with the MUP. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct to say that at no time in Operative Action Varivode was it suggested that you needed to have General Gotovina participate in assisting in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, I did not receive it from the Chief of Staff of Operation Varivode, to the effect that there was a need for such a thing. The staff or the headquarters was well capable of efficiently organising and implementing the action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. With respect -- that is -- was a specific question for Varivode. Generally speaking, the MUP and the military police had the compatibility of officially -- efficiently implementing investigative actions without having to involve the military in any investigation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only partially.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, are you saying that the -- the military police and the civilian police were not capable in their entirety of conducting and implementing investigative actions?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, if an investigation is underway against HV members for which there is reasonable doubt that they had perpetrated without close cooperation with their commanders who would make available to those included in the investigation the space they need for work, as well as to have the perpetrators available, then that cannot be efficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I didn't mean to suggest that you wouldn't need the cooperation of military people in a military investigation. What I'm saying is that in terms of leading an investigation, the military police and the civilian police were capable of leading and organizing investigative actions without having to involve the military in organizing an investigative action, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you include in the term "organisation"? If I am carrying out a crime investigation because there are reasonable grounds to believe that the members of a concern unit are the perpetrators of a certain crime, then it is only normal to expect that the commander as well as all of the officers of that unit cooperate closely with the officers and investigators. In that way, I introduce them as active participants in the investigation itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me use your language. You, in the military police, carry out the investigation, and then you seek the cooperation of military commanders in carrying out your investigation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If there is indicia that the perpetrators come from a unit or another organisational part of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, we're going to stick with OA Varivode for a few minutes. Mr. Registrar, if I could have - or Madam Registrar, I'm sorry - Exhibit D802, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you can flip through this, if you wish, Mr. Lausic. This is pursuant to your order of the 6th of October, which we just had on the screen. Here is one of the reports coming back in the action team about what they had done in the actions that were undertaken together with the MUP. It is sent directly to your attention, and if you flip through this, there are meetings are identified in point 1 to coordinate the work. You can turn the page. Check-points are being set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Turn to the second page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now let me take a step back here so there's no confusion. Operative Action Varivode was not just an investigation of the killing at Varivode, was it? It was a broader investigation. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not provide you with a precise answer. I would have to go back to the transcript as well as my witness statement, in which I answer that precisely. Since I was able to prepare myself, I answered therein how it was that the operative action Varivode came about. I believe it was because of the initiative of Mr. Benko who was Assistant minister of the interior in charge of the crime investigation police. He advised me of the case, but I cannot tell you anything on top of that without referring to the transcript itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think if we can take a look at this report and it might give you an indication about the scope of what OA Varivode was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So if we can go to page 3 in the English, please, which is -- and we're referring to numbered paragraph 3 in the original. Actually you can see the intro into paragraph 3 says: "Based on the presentation and overview of how the units were engaged, tasks were issued for a 12/12 work schedule. The formation of 14 duty patrol cars, daily visited by monitoring directing teams. Then if we go to section 3. "These are the results of OA Varivode from 0600 hours on 7 October to 2200 hours on 10 October: "Search the identification papers of 1282 HV members. 1050 HV vehicles were searched. 17 men were searched. Breakdown of HV members brought in for looting property. Broken it down by the various units in that three-day period." If we turn the page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The identity of 69 civilians was established. 28 were removed while attempting to steal property. 11 were warned. 9 were turned over to the MUP as persons caught perpetrating the criminal offence of stealing property. Confiscation of items. 15 disciplinary reports were submitted against HV members. Now, if I can ask you there, that's because one of the duties of the military police when you are able to identify a soldier whose engaged in some disciplinary offence whether at a check-point or someplace else, the military police completes a report and submits it to that soldier's commander to take disciplinary measures. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the bottom. There is much more detail throughout this, and I won't take the time to go through all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But it's clear -- the bottom of page 4, for example, which is the second paragraph -- right. They're both on the screen now. "The engagement of the crime investigation military police to shed light on these serious criminal offences began on 2 October 1995, when the first working meeting was held at 0830 hours attended by the administration of the RH MUP and military police administration staff. It was at that meeting that this service received its first information of the murders, based on which it then acted. Namely, the crime investigation military police was informed of 11 cases in which one or more civilians were murdered by unknown perpetrators."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Special emphasise" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think I'm working from a different copy; I apologise. If we scroll to the top of this page, please. To the top of the English page, please, and back in the original document, I think. I apologise. My mistake. It is numbered page 5 in the English at the top and -- correct. Can we scroll up further on top of the English page, please. Okay. I guess it's one page back then. Yes, I'm sorry. And if we can now go back one page in the B/C/S as well. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "Namely the crime investigation military police was informed of 11 cases in which one or more civilians were murdered by unknown perpetrators. Special emphasise was placed on cases with justified indications that the possible perpetrators or witnesses of a murder could have been members of the HV. "In only two cases information of a low level of verification concerning the participation of HV members was presented." And then it identifies the two --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, I'm sorry, in Croatian and in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "In the two that had some low level of verification were in" -- it says Gosic, but I believe the village is actually Gosic and Zrmanje. And then the conclusion was: "All other information pertaining to these or other murder cases pointing to possible involvement of HV members were of a much lower level of verification and did not warrant the involvement of military police crime investigators." Now, my question is: First, is it your recollection that the first time that the crime investigation military police received information about murders in the newly liberated areas was at a meeting on the 2nd of October, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I can confirm that. One of my basic remarks in my discussion with Mr. Benko, the Assistant Minister of the interior, was that we cannot act upon events of which we had not been notified. Later in the assessment of this operation, I also stressed the importance of acquainting the military police with certain events that we can act upon and in which we can get some results together in cooperation our colleagues from the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can turn the page in English, please, to the bottom of page 6. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, after operative action Varivode was launched, and three or four days into this operation, the conclusion was: "We conclude that after processing the crimes and undertaking other action under our jurisdiction and based received information of a low level of confirmation, we cannot talk about well founded indications that the perpetrators of unsolved murders were from the HV." And if we turn the page, you can see that it is signed and stamped by Colonel Damir Kozic. Now, do you recall as of 11 October 1995, was it the position of the military police crime investigation section that, in fact, "we could not talk about well-founded indications that the perpetrators of unsolved murders were members of the HV"?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite clear on your question. Do you want me to confirm the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is based on this report, which went to you, as of 11 October 1995, was it the conclusion of the military police administration with the information it had at that time that the allegations of -- that the perpetrators of unsolved murders were from the HV were not well founded?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't state in any precise terms about what I was thinking about it or the administration was thinking about it when we received the report. Since the report was submitted by one of the chiefs of one of the administrations of the military police, Colonel Kozic, as one of those who were in charge of Operation Varivode, of course, he was fully trusted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, another question is: This type of information about ongoing investigations of crime being committed by HV members, this report goes only to you, doesn't go to military commanders. Why doesn't it go to military commanders?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which military commanders do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I guess I'm particularly concerned about a certain Military District Commander. So let me ask you about Military District Commanders. Why didn't it go to them?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we can go back to the order establishing the staff of Operative Action Varivode, then I'd like to go back to that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's Exhibit P2189, please.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my order to the 71st and 72nd Battalions and to the chiefs of the military -- of the departments of the military police administration which contains quite precise and specific tasks about who the staff of the operative action will comprise, the modus operandi of the forces, the reserve forces, the reporting system. If we could go on to the next page, please. The order was sent to my higher up in the Ministry of Defence; the Assistant Minister of Defence; the minister of security; and to the minister of the interior, Mr. Moric. That was my chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's understood. My question or let me put to you. This information about ongoing investigations didn't go to General Gotovina because there was no need for that information to go to General Gotovina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing prevented the commanders of the 71st and 72nd Battalions, in their turn, to report in their own reports on the course of the action because it was supposed to say in what way they were using the human and materiel resources. And they were supposed to say what sort of results they achieved because they were very interesting to us. We saw that in the report, and this is something that a commander should definitely be interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me -- what somebody wasn't prevented from doing isn't the issue here. The issue is what you ordered, and if you felt that it was important that General Gotovina be involved in this operation and get information about this information -- about this operation, you would have put in the order that this information should be copied to General Gotovina. Right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one way of interpreting it. However, the operative action is taken over a certain territory, with a certain objective, and with certain forces. Primarily the individual who ordered such an action is the one to be reported to. However, since this task was to be implemented in the areas of responsibility of the 71st and 72nd Battalions, the commanders, in their daily reports, had to inform their own levels of command in their Military Districts both about the results and the course of the action. I believe that looking at the daily reports of the 72nd Battalion, one would actually see that all the actions and events would be indicated there, as were indicated here, concerning the check-points and the arrested members of the HV and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You just walked into my question next, Mr. Lausic. Because I don't think the daily reports actually reflect that. And we can take a look at P2183, which is the daily reports in October. And my next question to you was going to be why, in the daily reports, you don't have the results of the Operative Action Varivode.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Criminality" -- And, again, this is similar to what we saw yesterday was in the daily reports. A motor vehicle was stopped; somebody verbally and physically assaulted a Mr. Rajcic; a pistol was confiscated, et cetera. Go to the next point. Four soldiers got into a fight with a civilian. Zupanic sustained serious injuries in his stomach area and was hospitalised. We can flip through these. Mr. Lausic, but these type of reports aren't the results of Operation Action Varivode being reported to the Split Military District Command about what your criminal police was investigating and the results. So let me put to you again. The information about ongoing criminal investigations was something that was being reported up to the military police administration. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, but, first of all, I have to say that you read out the events which transpired on the 1st and 2nd October, and the report we were looking at was a summary report concerning the period between 6th and 10th of October, I mean the report submitted by Colonel Kozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can get you those dates as well. And while we're pulling that up, let me ask you the next question I was going ask you which is, something -- have you ever seen a daily report in the military police said, We have a suspicion that somebody -- some HV soldier committed a crime, but we don't know what to do.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. A query addressed to me from whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: These reports are reports of what happened after the military police took action. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There is an system and a procedure prescribed by rules and law, once a perpetrator has been entered into the system by the military police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There is nothing for a commander to do on the basis of this report except wait for the process, the system to run its course, whether it's the criminal justice system, the disciplinary courts, et cetera, unless a disciplinary complaint has been brought to the attention of the commander, as I indicated to you earlier this morning, that the military police would also send a report to the commander to ask him to take action to -- to assert a disciplinary measure.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Misetic, but I personally believe you are completely wrong. Let us go back to one event we can see on our screens, under item 3. "On the 2nd of October, 1995, at 0400 hours soldiers Stipica Babic member of the military post 2136 Split brought to the dormitory of the barracks of Saint Nikola in Split a civilian "MM," aged 19 from Split. And by use of physical force, commented rape on the same person. A patrol of the 72nd Military Police Battalion soldier Babic in and took him into custody. And the officers of the criminal investigation department of the military police of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, Split, will bring the perpetrator before an investigating judge with a criminal report. One always starts from the causes preceding the commission of a crime. If we're talking about this particular case, the circumstances favourable to the commission of this crime is that -- the violation of rules prescribed by the military police. One of them being the unauthorised entry into the barracks of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that we're moving far away from what the question is about. What Mr. Misetic, from what I understand, would like to know is, to what extent these reports, if they would be sent to the military command structure, what -- whether these reports were to require them to take any follow-up action, rather than just see how the process that had started would make further progress, just an observing position rather than any action to be taken upon. Now, it may be that the beginning of why a crime was committed that this is a matter of lack of discipline which may have consequences in general for restoring discipline. But on these specific cases if you would send them to the military commanders, you wouldn't expect them to do anything apart from reading it and say, Oh, okay, is what happened, and what will happen next in the proceedings. That's what Mr. Misetic would like to know, whether you would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I've just answered Mr. Misetic's question by telling him that I believe him to be completely wrong. The cause of the criminal offence and the processing is the violation of the rules of service of the armed forces. On the basis of this first report, the commander is entitled to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let me stop you here for a second. Because, otherwise, we are at risk to move far away from the question again. You say Mr. Misetic is wrong. So if this would be sent to a military commander, then he would have to take some action. Now, what action would you expect -- take one of the examples, what action should be taken by a military commander if he would have received the information about, for example, the rape you just mentioned? What would he have to do on the basis of this report if he would have received it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. He would have to designate the officer who would be in charge of the disciplinary investigation, or, rather, scene of crime investigation. The officer would take all the actions required to establish the facts of the case; that is, whether the rules of service or some other rules of the armed forces were violated, that officer would submit a report to the commander on the disciplinary investigation that was conducted. And on the basis of that report, if the investigation were to indicate that there was a breach of discipline involved, he would be duty-bound to impose disciplinary measure. But if the investigation were to show that the -- a major breach of discipline was involved, the disciplinary charges would be brought against that soldier before a disciplinary court. The upshot of that could be that the soldier, if he is an active serviceman of the Croatian army, could be dishonourably discharged, et cetera. All these actions can be taken without awaiting the end of the court proceedings initiated for that particular criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, now, you have said that I'm completely wrong; and I'm going to say that you're completely wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's one to one. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Look at Article 15 of the rule, Mr. Lausic. Let's stick to the rules. Now what the military police is supposed to do -- if we could have P880 on the screen please. Article 15 says: "The military police has the following powers."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Page 8 in the English, please; page 7 in the B/C/S. And it's subsection 3. It should be the next page in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now: "Members of the military police submit a disciplinary report against military personnel who violate military discipline and a criminal report against persons who commit a crime that falls within the jurisdiction of a military court." Now the question I put to is, on the basis of the daily report if a -- if it's a disciplinary infraction that led to the criminal activity, then it was your military police that was responsible for submitting the criminal report and the disciplinary report to the relevant commander. The commander doesn't have to look at the daily report and assume that your military police didn't do what it was supposed to do under the rules.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I don't find the question clear. The reporting of the commander on such an event which would contain these facts, wouldn't that fulfil the requirements under the rule to submit disciplinary -- a disciplinary report or bring disciplinary charges? Well, of course, a report on the event ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, there seems to be a lot of confusion. Let focus on the example of the rape, as we find it, under item 3 in this October report. You were asked what the use would be of sending this report to a military commander, what follow-up would they have to give to that? You explained that he had to take action so that it would be investigated by someone designated to do a disciplinary investigation. Were the -- was there any violation of the rules of discipline? Now -- so that would have been the purpose of sending it to the military commander, who, as you said, doesn't just sit back and wait what happens, but you said he would have to take action. Now Mr. Misetic takes you to this rule which says that if there's a violation of military discipline and in cases it amounts to a crime, it is the military police who will investigate and will report, take the case to the extent necessary to the investigating judge and bring them to the -- into the military judicial system, and report on the violation of discipline to the commander. Clearly indicating that Mr. Misetic disagrees with you that the commander who receives a report like this one would need it take any action because he doesn't have to designate anyone to do the investigation for disciplinary proceedings because the report on that violation of -- of the rules of discipline, he would receive that anyhow without taking any action because it was the task of the military police. So that seems to keep the both of you apart. Mr. Misetic says that's exactly what the military police does: They take care of both follow up in terms of criminal procedure of bringing the case to court, and they would also take care of reporting to the commander about the violation of rules of discipline. Now you say, no, nevertheless it would be useful to receive this report because you have to take action in view of preparing whether any disciplinary measures have to be taken. No, says Mr. Misetic, that's done by the military police as well. They just deliver their results of their investigations to the commander. Could you, please, comment where Mr. Misetic, if I have understood you well, is wrong and why you are right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The disciplinary proceedings are always conducted by the commander either through a disciplinary investigation at the end of which, if a minor breach of discipline, disciplinary measure is imposed, or where a major breach of discipline is involved, then there are disciplinary charges brought. It -- and this is always conducted by the commander of the unit, the member of which is a suspect of having breached the rules of service. And it is the officers of the criminal investigation department of the military police who carry out the investigation, at the end of which they report the results to the commander, and send a copy of the -- send to him a copy of the criminal report that they had sent to the military -- to the relevant competent military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, wouldn't it be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Misetic, I'd like it put on the record that the Chamber was informed by the OTP that there would be no applications for protective measures for the 92 quater statements which were admitted in the decision of the 16th of January of this year. And similarly, that -- but that's after seven months and 14 days that the same would be true for the 92 quater statements that were admitted on the 16th of June of last year. Mr. Tieger, is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is my understanding, Your Honour. I hope you don't think we rushed things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No concerns about that at this moment. Well, I introduced the matter, so perhaps that it was totally superfluous to remind you of the 14 days, but perhaps it was not totally superfluous. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, we have found these October daily reports but let me just refresh everyone's recollection by taking you to Exhibit D802 first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, can we go to page 3 in the English, which is page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think we've got a LiveNote -- well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, we can do these totals, but this is again OA Varivode from 0600 hours on 7 October to 2200 hours on 10 October. Then the fourth indented point is "HV members brought in for looting property," and there are the different units. And if we turn the page in English and scroll down in the Croatian, it says that 36 HV members, which is the total, were brought there for looting property.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we turn the page in Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, there's an entry there. You see it says: "15 disciplinary reports were submitted against HV members." Now, why does the military police submit disciplinary reports?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you perhaps hinting at the possibility that commanders have -- that they can initiate disciplinary proceedings, and commanders alone? Well, yes, in that case that would be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction it is up to the military police according to the rules of work of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the military police that can submit disciplinary reports. If there are reasons to suspect that there were breaches of discipline or rules of service, that is an obligation on to itself for the commander to initiate disciplinary proceedings, as well irrespective of what kind of information he received from the military police in the specific case of rape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... It was just a general question first, Mr. Lausic. Now, I want to get to the 36 soldiers brought in for looting between the 7th and the 10th October. And you raise the issue of daily reports, so let's take a look at those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, please, it is P2183, beginning at page 10 in the English and page 6 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask Madam Registrar to flip through the entries in the daily reports for the 6th -- for the 7th, 8th, 9th. And 10th. And I want to tell me where, if you think you see report being these 36 soldiers being brought in for looting. So, for example, the 7th of October, in paragraph 2, a member of a unit from Zagreb under the influence of alcohol got into a verbal and physical fight with his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can we turn the page, please. In English as well, please. Scroll at the top it may be a entry -- there we go. And also in the English, please. It's the 6th, so if we can scroll down, pleases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On the 8th under the section criminality, soldier Milosevic for reasons that have not yet been established fired one round from a semi-automatic rifle in the direction of Sergeant Vagner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn the page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On the 7th of October at an intersection, conscript Josip Stimac in the company of civilians intercepted civilians from Zagreb, and while threatening them with a kitchen knife, misappropriated 140 Kunas and five audiotapes." On the 8th at 1920 in front of the Kvaternik barracks in Gospic, a soldier by -- Balenovic [phoen] while heavily intoxicated intentionally fired one round from an automatic rifle issued to him into his left shin. Now, if you wish, I can go on and on with these types of examples. But there's no entry here for the 36 soldiers who were brought in for looting. Now, can you explain why those 36 soldiers wouldn't have been in a daily report?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Misetic, you are showing a daily summary report of security-related events drafted by the service duty of the MP administration. This is not a daily report of the 71st or the 72nd Battalion, depending on where the incidents occurred. As can be seen from the report of Colonel Kozic, there were dozens of controlled check-points established. The duty service and this daily summary security report in the categories contained, reports to the highest instances on the most important events pertaining to crime, breaches of discipline, security of military traffic, and other security-related events. I think those were the items. Based on the reports of MP units, the duty officer extracts the most important events, given their modus operandi, or the victim, or the perpetrator, or with a view to establishing certain other circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... is it your suggestion that the bringing in of 36 soldiers for looting in a four-day period wasn't as important as a soldier shooting himself in the shin? Why wouldn't 36 soldiers being brought in for looting over a four-day period be significant enough to be in this report?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a single item, yes. But they came in successfully, as they were being caught with misappropriated property throughout the time-period and at various locations. The value of the property varied as well, as well as some other circumstances. In order for me to give you a precise answer, I would have to go through all of the reports of the 71st and 72nd MP Battalions in relation to this period in order to be able to respond to the question which was, whether the daily reports encompassed these events as Mr. Kozic did in his summary report when he sent it to me, reporting on the four days and summarizing the results of Operative Action Varivode.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, if necessary, I'll take you through a different example, but you've now indicated that you think maybe there's different daily reports for the 72nd MP Battalion. Let's spend some time on this, since it was the subject of your direct examination, but ... let's look at the daily reports of the 72nd MP Battalion for the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which is, Madam Registrar, 65 ter 6974.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the report that would go, again, to Military District, the prosecutors, military court. If you read through that. There is a shooting from an automatic rifle in Zadar. Military police came to the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Breaches of the provisions of the rules of military discipline, no events reported." That's on -- if we can turn the page, unless there's -- there might be something else in there that you might want it take a look at. But it's a traffic accident again. This's the daily report of the 8th. And I would also like you to take a look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, the same procedure, I tender it, unless it's on the Prosecution's bar table submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is it on the bar table submission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it's understood there's no objections against admission. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could, Madam Registrar, take look at the daily report for the next day, on the 9th, which is 65 ter 6961, please. The 9th, criminality -- crime, I should say, nothing to report. Breaches of the provisions of the rules of military discipline, nothing to report. Other events. Somebody was driving at a high rate of speed and hit a pedestrian. So these are those daily reports of the 72nd MP Battalion that you reference. Now, I'd like to turn your attention to Exhibit D866, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Madam Registrar, I made a mistake. It should be D868.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now this is a list of temporarily confiscated items at check-points in the zone of responsibility of the 5th Company of the military police, Sinj, which is part of the 72nd MP Battalion, and it's a report for the -- from the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is a report of all the items that are seized at the check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn the page again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: TVs, videos, refrigerators, et cetera. Now my question for you is: Items are being seized at check-points, the military police is taking action to confiscate items, but that is not reflected in the daily reports. My question is, why?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will be very cautious in my answer, given the terminology I intend to use. Because, unfortunately, then a daily report would resemble a phone book. By that I mean the sheer amount of things that had to be encompassed by any given daily report. The daily report mentions the most specific events from the point of view of the categories envisaged, the breaches of discipline, road traffic safety, et cetera, et cetera. As for any action like this one, a report was surely submitted to the unit commander to which that particular soldier belonged to. We can see that the military police administration and its duty service was always compiling reports of nine different MP battalions, which, in turn, made summary reports from each of their respective 50 different organisational elements. Only the most important events are mentioned, be it from the point of view of the way that offences were committed or if there were victims or the perpetrators were of a certain nature, that goes into the summary, and that's why it's called summary of security-related events in the past 24 hours. I neither confirm nor deny that the commander of that particular unit involved was informed on each and every single event or was not informed. As for in what way and form, that I can't say. That would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. But my question to you is: Do you agree that just because something wasn't in a daily report wouldn't be reason for someone to conclude that the military police wasn't doing its job in terms of other activities?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be extremely unfair to say that the military police did only what is contained in the summary of daily events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And the military police did many other activities that wouldn't be in the daily reports. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yesterday there was an example of this. You showed us a copy from the duty service register of the 4th Company of the 72nd Battalion, if I'm not mistaken. We saw a few entries, reflecting a whole spectrum of activities which one could not find in the daily summary report of the 4th Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one or two additional questions, in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This list dated the 8th of August of items that were temporarily confiscated, would that be the result of one day activity, or would it be for more days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President. I would have to see the introductory part of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we move to the cover page. It reads that it's "report on items temporarily confiscated at check-points in the zone of responsibility of the 5th Company of the military police, Sinj." More days? One day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, I'd like to draw your attention to the following. This report bears the date of the 8th of August. In the first paragraph, those submitting the report state the following: "By authorised officials and as of the points when the offensive operation ceased and the occupied territories were liberated in the area of responsibility of the 5th Company of the military police of Sinj, the following objects were temporarily seized." This means that -- it includes the preceding three or four days. Three, I suppose. I cannot be more precise than that. In any case, given the date of the report and the first paragraph, I believe it includes at least three days of work at the check-points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although -- do we have that in our translation? It seem that just a portion is missing, or am I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's missing. And, again, I do recall this being a 65 ter so -- and there's an OTP number on the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Again, someone has translated, but didn't consider it important enough to translate this portion as well, apparently. It's not one word, it's three full lines which explains the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll get it corrected and uploaded in e-court, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have one or two more questions on this document. Temporarily confiscating, could you explain what is, in fact, meant. This Chamber has heard evidence that not always the documents that were confiscated or temporarily confiscated were always kept in possession of those who had confiscated them, that sometimes it was left in the hands of those from whom it was confiscated. Could you comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the military police took over its model of activity from the civilian police, as well as certain forms, printed forms used by the civilian police. By the same token, we printed the form entitled "Temporarily Confiscated Items." Those forms are made in three copies, in triplicate, irrespective of what the object concerned is, in this case, it would be different types of property starting with vehicles and -- down to house appliances or tools. However, some of these objects can also be the objects with which crimes had been perpetrated, as well as illegal substances, narcotics. All of that is entered in the form which is then signed by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, you give a lot of details on who signed and from the back of the page. What I was interested in is, were all these well over 200 items, as you see them here, would all those items be handed over to those who temporarily confiscated them? Or was there any chance that some were left in the hands of those who carried those goods when they were confiscated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I thought you were asking me to clarify the word, "temporary" or "temporarily." That is why I began with a comprehensive answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you then now continue with the other part of my question, whether they were actually taken in the hands of those who confiscated the items.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The objects were taken away. In keeping with my order, which is in the documents, if the objects concerned could be used in military units, they were handed over to the logistics departments of military units or another organisational structure of the Croatian army. If the objects concerned could not be used by the armed forces, they were handed over to civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Civilian authorities being who, in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The civilian authorities in the newly liberated area were the municipal services or government commissioners designated to certain areas and their competent services and departments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want to say if there was no need for these goods to use them by military authorities, they were passed on to the civilian authorities for using them. Could I imagine a television set to be given to a welfare service, so as to provide it to -- to an elderly home or something like that? Is that how I have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be one way of understanding it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What would be the other way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the sense that the civilian authorities have such items handed over by the military police at their disposal to make use of them as they see fit. They could also be handed over to the families of displaced persons whose homes need furnishing, et cetera. We did not really go into the ways in which the civilian authorities would be making use of such items. Our priority was to make sure that we disposed of such items as they would constitute a burden a given MP unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So they were not stored for further -- further proceedings, but they were distributed military if for -- if there was any military need to use them; civilian, if the remainder would be useful for the civilian services. Could I then ask you, cars, vehicles, motor vehicles, were they usually used by the military; or were they often passed to the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I first be allowed to answer the question that was put to me first? In order to ascertain the -- who the owner of the appropriated item was -- well, this had to be done because one always had to know who the aggravated party of a given crime of theft was. That was the precondition in order to initiate proceedings for that particular crime. In the cases, such as this one, complaints we received from -- or, rather, the information we received from the persons who were in possession of these items was that they collected them on the way, that the items had been discarded, and so on and so forth. Now to answer your latter question, there were such instances where the vehicles concerned remained in possession of the Croatian army for their purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, we see a lot of cars and a lot of equipment. For cars, were they ever returned to the rightful owners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the follow-up actions aimed at identifying the owners of these cars, we tried to ascertain who they were, and if an owner was identified, efforts were made at returning the vehicles to the rightful owner. In the years following 1995, especially once the authorities resumed control of the entire liberated area in 1997, many of the citizens who had fled the region and which were covered by Operation Storm and returned to the Republic of Croatia, filed and many of them are still filing requests for some of their property to be returned to them. In most cases, since it is impossible to return their rightful property to them, they receive compensation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, how many cars are you aware of were returned to the civilian owners from which they had been taken or stolen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wouldn't be able to give that you information. I can see under number 1 here, Mercedes truck with the UN licence plates. In other words, a vehicle used by the forces of UNPROFOR. I believe that that particular vehicle was returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And my question was not about UN vehicles but about civilians. Are you aware of one single car taken from a civilian or stolen from a civilian person that was returned to that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have information to that effect, but I wouldn't be able to tell you anything specific, in terms of the location involved or the individual involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, similarly, for cars taken or stolen, are you -- could you give us any detail on one case where compensation has been paid to that person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. A returnee of Serbian ethnicity who returned to the Republic of Croatia filed a request for indemnity listing all the items that were taken away from him. And the judicial bodies of the Republic of Croatia, who were seized of his lawsuit, resolved the case in -- in a positive way. That's to say, in favour of him being paid an indemnity. Let me tell you how it is that I came to know this. I'm referring to the period up until 2003, at which time I was the chief of the military police administration. The judicial bodies would be seeking information from both the military police and the civilian police about whether any of the items that the injured party listed as having been taken away from him at the location where he resided, had been confiscated. Alternatively, they were seeking to receive information about the units that were in combat in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- one additional question. How many of these requests, approximately, you dealt with until 2003? 10, 100, 1.000, 20 -- something, give -- if you could, could you give me a rough figure of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't be precise. In the early days, such requests or such lawsuits were few and far between, and then they grew in intensity. There were dozens of them. And according to the latest information I have, something I learned from the grapevine was that the situation was such that the justice administration is flooded with such indemnity claims in relation to the items that had been taken away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was: How many such requests you dealt with until 2003. You said I can't be precise. I asked you to give a rough figure. Was it 10? Was it more than 10? Was it less than 10? Was it only the one you just mentioned? Could you please give me an estimate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were up to a dozen cases at the time when I was still active as the chief of the administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean over those eight years since 1995 until 2003?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it grew in frequency as of 2000. I don't recall there having been as many such claims before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question simply was when you say up to a dozen cases, I'm just verifying with you if that was, as you said, when you were still active as the chief of the administration, is it correct that that was in 2003. So that was between 1995 and 2003. Thank you for those answers. No, I have one additional question. We see for a couple of days - may have been they or four - well over 200 items. The days the reports that followed, were they of similar length? Or did they contain more items per three or four days? Or were they reported on a daily basis? Could you give us a indication.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The activity aimed at preventing the commission of such crimes and confiscating the items that had been taken away definitely continued. Between late September and through to the end -- through to October, the number dwindled. One can provide summary information only once he's got information from his colleagues of the Ministry of the Interior, since our presence in the area was gradually reduced as the civilian police increased their presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I must admit, I do not know the English word "to dwindle." Could someone help me out so that I -- is it reduce?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I thought. But I didn't know the word. Would I then have to understand that by late September and through October that then the frequency reduced? Is that how I have to understand your answer? I am aware, Mr. Misetic, that I took up more than 15 minutes of -- well, not of your time, but of the time available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we have to stop for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could just note -- advise the Chamber for the record. In terms of the daily reports for the -- you had asked about whether this was a summary for three days. Those daily reports are also on the Prosecution's bar table submission, and I can tell you that I don't think that you'll find that they're any different than the ones that you've already seen today. But the Chamber will be able to examine them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You Honour will recollect that they are part of the stipulation made between the Prosecution and the Cermak Defence team during Mr. Theunens's testimony. I produced them in cross-examination to him. We made a stipulation, and then we have submitted to the Court those documents that we were able to obtain in the EDS system on the same matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's documents, of course, I asked the witness about what his recollection was, and I asked him to give further information about it. Then if there is no other urgent further procedural matter, then, Mr. Lausic, I'd like to again instruct you not to speak with anyone about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given, and I'd like you to follow Madam Usher because I will just put one or two questions to the parties. And we'd like to see you back on Monday morning. We expect you back on Monday morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I expected.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether to restart. It certainly was not part of his testimony, so let's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I'd like to know where approximately you are. Of course, the Chamber is aware that getting short concrete answers is not easiest thing to achieve with this witness, but could you give us an indication as where we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would certainly think I will be finished by the end of the first session on Monday, and hopefully earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any change in the assessment made by the other parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. One day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. One section at least -- at most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Chamber has an impression how we could proceed. We will adjourn, and we will resume on Monday, the 2nd of February, at 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
